title: A Typewriter for the Lantern
premise: In 1917, Sebastian 'Seb' Lockridge drives for suffragist organizer Edith Marlowe and secretly reads every letter she delivers, memorizing the network of names in a small-town movement. When the army requisitions the town to build a munitions depot, it seizes the ledger holding every name — and begins rewriting the record of who resisted and who vanished. Seb, whose own identity is a careful fiction, must reconstruct the truth from memory and smuggle it into print before the victors' historians seal the official version. She succeeds at terrible cost: the book is published under a dead man's name, her own history is erased from it, and she chooses that erasure as the price of everyone else's survival.
about_author: Sebastian Quintana is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing requisitioned municipal records from the First World War. They write historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Route
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Establishes Seb's double life: driver by day, reader of every letter by night, keeper of names no one knows she keeps. She copies addresses into her own hidden notebook. Emotional beat: quiet competence masking loneliness; she belongs everywhere and nowhere.

chapters.title: Edith's Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Edith Marlowe entrusts Seb with transporting the master ledger of members, donors, and correspondents. Seb realizes the ledger contains her own assumed name — proof she exists only on paper. Beat: intimacy and dread entwined.

chapters.title: Requisition Notice
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Soldiers post notices: the town is taken for a munitions depot; residents have two weeks; all records are seized for 'security review.' Neighbors react with fear and collaboration. Beat: the ordinary world cracks open.

chapters.title: What the Sergeant Reads
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Army clerks inventory confiscated papers; Seb watches a sergeant skim the ledger with bored efficiency and understands names will become charges. She memorizes faces and filing order. Beat: cold fear sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: The Driver They Kept
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. The army retains local drivers; Seb volunteers, trading access for suspicion. Inside the requisitioned hall she sees the ledger boxed for transport to the capital. Beat: loyalty tested — serving the occupiers to serve the truth.

chapters.title: Letters That Never Arrived
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Delivering army mail, Seb finds intercepted letters from townspeople, including pleas from women Edith organized. She begins copying them verbatim into her notebook. Beat: grief transmuted into documentation.

chapters.title: A Name Not Hers
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. An officer questions 'Sebastian Lockridge'; her papers hold because a dead brother's identity shields her. Flashback to how she built this self. Beat: identity as armor and prison.

chapters.title: The Printer's Daughter
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Seb seeks out Nell Ashcombe, whose father ran the town press before seizure. Nell hates Edith for reasons Seb must hear and absorb. Beat: friction; allies are not simple.

chapters.title: The Historian Arrives
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Captain Voss, an official historian, arrives to write the campaign's account — courteous, meticulous, and already drafting a version where resistance never happened. He interviews Seb. Beat: the antagonist revealed as a rival author of reality.

chapters.title: Night Copying
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Seb and Nell secretly rebuild the ledger from memory, intercepted letters, and Nell's father's hidden type slugs. Errors haunt them; a wrong name could hang someone. Beat: obsessive, terrified craftsmanship.

chapters.title: The Missing Page
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. A crucial page — naming a protected informant inside the army — is missing from Seb's memory. She must return to the requisitioned hall. Beat: moral vertigo; retrieving truth may betray a person.

chapters.title: Inside the Filing Room
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Seb infiltrates the records office during an air-raid blackout, finds the page, and discovers Voss has annotated it: he knows more than he performs. Beat: triumph curdling into exposure.

chapters.title: Voss Offers a Version
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Voss privately reveals he suspects her; offers immunity and a flattering paragraph in his history if she surrenders the reconstructed record. Beat: temptation articulated perfectly — truth preserved but owned.

chapters.title: Edith Returns
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Edith, presumed evacuated, reappears disguised, demanding the ledger be used to force a public trial, whatever the cost to the network. Mentor and protégé split over means. Beat: loyalty vs. truth made flesh.

chapters.title: Nell's Betrayal
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Under pressure, Nell's brother informs on the copying operation; soldiers raid the print shop. The manuscript survives by minutes; Nell is taken. Beat: guilt, rage, and the cost of slow work in fast times.

chapters.title: The Bargain With Ghosts
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Seb weighs trading herself for Nell via Voss's offer. She visits the mass requisition lists and finds her brother's real death recorded — her false identity was built on a true grave. Beat: identity collapses into mourning.

chapters.title: Typesetting by Candlelight
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Final assembly of the account in the ruined press: names, letters, dates, including Edith's methods and Seb's own deceptions — everything, unflattering included. Beat: resolve; truth without mercy or omission.

chapters.title: The Train South
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Seb rides the mail train carrying printed sheets sewn into mail sacks, pursued by Voss's clerk. A near-search resolved by an unexpected soldier's silence. Beat: breathless suspense; strangers choosing conscience.

chapters.title: What Voss Prints
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Voss publishes first: an official history, elegant and hollow, citing 'no significant dissent.' Seb reads it in a safehouse and understands the race was always against narrative, not arrest. Beat: despair before defiance.

chapters.title: A Typewriter for the Lantern
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. In a lantern-lit cellar, a sympathetic editor types the final fair copy of the true account, striking Seb's name from it at her insistence so no one can be traced through her. Beat: sacrifice as authorship.

chapters.title: The Record Holds
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Years later, a parliamentary inquiry cites the anonymous pamphlet; Nell is freed; Edith disavows the radical tactics but confirms every name. Voss's edition quietly loses authority. Beat: vindication without victory lap.

chapters.title: Signed, Nobody
chapters.summary: POV Sebastian. Elderly Seb, living under yet another name, receives a letter addressed only to 'the driver who read the letters.' She does not answer, but she opens her old notebook and adds one line: her real name, finally written down. Beat: quiet restoration of self.
